chapter_endings: I'd find where it was in the morning.

I slept the poor thin sleep of a chair, and somewhere in it, near the bottom, I heard the telephone in the hall, or dreamed I heard it, not ringing, only the line, the long flat note of an open line, very faint, going on and on in the cold with no hand on it, as though somewhere a receiver lay off its cradle, and the tone went out into the house and waited, the way it had waited for me, slow, patient, listening, for someone to lift the other end and answer.
The cold was almost a relief.
And to go higher than five.
I didn't yet know whose list I was reading my way toward, or that the mercy in it had run out a long time ago, in this house, for a great many, before ever I came.

And I sat with the marbles in my pocket and did not take them out, and I did not let myself think the name that was pushing at the lid of the drawer I keep shut, the name of a boy who had grey flannel shorts and a tin of marbles and a red one he always took, the name I hadn't said aloud in thirty years and wouldn't say in that house, not yet, not for anything.

I went and slept in the kitchen with the lamp up and the crate open behind me in the dark, and I didn't write down the thing I understood, which was that I had stopped being the one who sealed the crates.
That much was true.

And I sat with the marbles cold in my pocket against my leg, nineteen of them, one red, and I did not say the name of the boy whose foot was that size, who went into the water once and was never found, and who had climbed the stairs tonight, dripping, toward the only warm room in his great-aunt's freezing house.

I sat down in the kitchen chair where I'd slept two nights and I put my hands flat on the cold table and I looked at the gray light coming up over the pond through the window I wouldn't go nearer, and I waited, and I didn't know what for, and the slow tone in the hall, when I listened for it, was no longer the line.

I sat with the marbles cold against my leg, nineteen of them, one red, and I held the lamp in my lap like a thing that might keep me warm, and the gray came up slow at the window, and somewhere below the trees the water lay under its skin of ice with whatever stood at the edge of it, and I sat with my back to the dark and waited for a morning I had no reason left to think would help me.
I'd spent thirty years thinking the farmer meant the pond.

I turned the key in the case and left it locked, which was foolish, a lock won't hold what opens my own sealed crates, but I turned it anyway, and stood up out of the chair I don't sit in, and the day was a working day with nothing in it I could work.
He was written down.

Below the sash the pond lay flat and grey beneath its new ice, eighty yards down a slope that began five feet inside a wall, and I picked up the plan and the cold tape and went out into the honest chill of the landing, and didn't measure anything else that day.
I was the last entry in it, not yet called.

I sat at the kitchen table in the last of the day with the closed notebook under my hand and the cold marbles in my pocket, and outside the snow turned to the sound of rain on the snow, a soft endless seething against the black glass, and somewhere down the lane, in the dark I couldn't see into, the culvert was filling.
And so, with the road gone into the flood and nothing left on the list to strike, did I.

I left the warm room when there was nothing more to see, and I went down the stairs in the dark, and the warm came with me a little way and then let me go to the cold, and behind me the chair kept its seat and the window kept the pond and the depths kept their shape under the new white lid, and the rest of it waited, with all its order, for me to come down to the pond in the morning of my own accord.
I didn't turn, and I didn't turn, and I didn't turn.

I stayed there with the lamp going down toward its last finger of oil and my palm on the closed cover and the rain pouring easy through the broken place where the bridge had been, and I didn't get up, and I didn't turn the lamp higher, and I faced the dark ahead of me the way I'd faced the page: name set, year set, the one column left empty, waiting only for the hand to come back and write what I am.
I stayed in the dying light and reckoned it, as she had reckoned hers, and found I was not going to pay it.
